title: Allowable Complex Black Holes in the Euclidean Gravitational Path Integral
text:
Motivation and setup
The gravitational path integral provides a way to calculate black-hole thermodynamics by summing over spacetime geometries. Its practical successes raise a difficult question: which geometries belong in that sum? Supersymmetric black holes make the question particularly sharp. The Euclidean solutions used to compute their protected partition function have complex metrics. Requiring an ordinary real, positive-definite geometry would discard precisely the saddle points needed for the calculation.
The starting point is the Euclidean gravitational path integral, written in the paper as equation (1):
\[
\mathcal{Z}=\int\mathcal{D}g_{\mu\nu}\mathcal{D}\Psi\,e^{-I_{E}[g_{\mu\nu},\Psi]}~,
\]
Here \(g_{\mu\nu}\) describes geometry, \(\Psi\) denotes the remaining fields, and \(I_E\) is their Euclidean action. Boundary conditions specify the observable being computed. In a semiclassical treatment, this formal integral is approximated by contributions from saddle points. Finding a solution of the equations of motion, however, does not by itself establish that the solution is an admissible contribution.
This work tests a proposed admissibility rule against an independent boundary-theory calculation. The setting is type IIB string theory on asymptotically \(AdS_5\times S^5\), dual to \(\mathcal{N}=4\) supersymmetric Yang–Mills theory. The analysis allows two unequal angular momenta while restricting the three electric charges to be equal. The observable is the superconformal index, a protected trace whose non-supersymmetric contributions cancel. Its convergence can be constrained directly from the spectrum of the boundary theory.
In particular, supersymmetric derivatives generate arbitrarily large angular momentum. Their contributions must be suppressed, requiring the renormalized angular chemical potentials to have positive real parts. This is equation (15):
\[
\operatorname{Re}(\Omega_{a,b}^{\prime})>0\,.
\]
There are additional positivity conditions on the regulator and electric chemical potentials. Together they define the region where the index has its statistical interpretation. The gravitational question is whether the geometry itself recognizes these boundaries.

title: Allowable Complex Black Holes in the Euclidean Gravitational Path Integral
text:
Construction and results
The test uses the Kontsevich–Segal–Witten, or KSW, criterion. It asks whether auxiliary real matter fields have appropriately convergent kinetic terms on a complex background. For every real, nonzero \(p\)-form \(F\), the pointwise requirement is equation (19):
\[
\mathrm{Re}\left(\sqrt{\det g}\,g^{i_{1}j_{1}}\ldots g^{i_{p}j_{p}}F_{i_{1}\ldots i_{p}}F_{j_{1}\ldots j_{p}}\right)>0~,
\]
This condition ranges over the allowed form degrees, including the scalar case. It is a local test throughout spacetime rather than a comparison of the total actions of different black holes. For a diagonal form of the complex metric, it has the equivalent expression given in equation (20):
\[
\sum_{i}|\arg\lambda_{i}|<\pi~.
\]
The \(\lambda_i\) are the diagonal metric entries after the appropriate change of basis. They should not be confused with ordinary eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix: the metric is complex symmetric, and it transforms by congruence. The paper develops a practical procedure using real symmetric matrices and a generalized eigenvalue problem, avoiding that ambiguity.
The black-hole solutions are analytically continued to finite-temperature complex Euclidean saddles with supersymmetric boundary conditions. The analysis begins near the asymptotic boundary, where the expressions simplify. The scalar condition reproduces positivity of the real part of the inverse temperature. The one-form condition yields the angular-potential inequalities already required by convergence of the index. At the angular poles, the higher-form tests do not impose additional restrictions beyond the lower-form conditions.



Original Figure 1: The three panels test the asymptotic one-form condition at different polar angles, at fixed \(r_*=0.1\). Requiring the condition at every angle selects the region between the red boundaries, where the index converges. All panels are reproduced from the paper.


The full geometry requires more than an asymptotic test. Numerical checks examine finite radii and several polar angles, applying the scalar, one-form, and higher-form conditions sequentially. In these scans the strongest restrictions arise at the asymptotic boundary and the two angular poles. The higher-form conditions introduce no stronger boundary in the tested bulk region. The resulting allowed set agrees with the convergence region identified independently in the field theory.

title: Allowable Complex Black Holes in the Euclidean Gravitational Path Integral
text:
Interpretation and limits



Original Figure 2: All twelve panels are retained. Moving down the rows approaches the asymptotic boundary; moving across the columns changes the polar angle. The green region becomes most restrictive at infinity and at the poles. The red curves mark the index-convergence boundaries, from the paper.


The location of the failure carries physical information. It occurs far from the black-hole core and is associated with one angular-momentum component. That pattern is consistent with a grey galaxy: a central black hole accompanied by a distant, dilute gas carrying a macroscopic share of the angular momentum. The standard single-center saddle ceases to be an adequate description in precisely the region where a two-component phase is expected to matter.
The result is a detailed test in a specific sector, with analytic boundary calculations supported by numerical bulk checks. It is not a universal proof that KSW identifies every physical gravitational saddle. The criterion studies auxiliary-field fluctuations, excludes metric fluctuations and backreaction, and can be too weak in other settings. In particular, the related two-charge \(AdS_4\) analysis finds an instability that KSW does not detect. The paper also distinguishes numerical evidence from analytic proof in checking positivity of certain chemical-potential factors across parameter space.
A complete Euclidean saddle describing the supersymmetric black-hole-plus-gas phase remains an open problem. The present analysis identifies where the familiar saddle becomes inadmissible; it does not construct the replacement geometry. This separation between a diagnostic and a full description is central to interpreting the result.

title: Supersymmetric Grey Galaxies, Dual Dressed Black Holes and the Superconformal Index
text: Skip to main content

title: Supersymmetric Grey Galaxies, Dual Dressed Black Holes and the Superconformal Index
text:
Motivation and setup
Black-hole entropy is a count of microscopic states, but identifying exactly which states are counted can be subtle. In strongly coupled \(\mathcal{N}=4\) Yang–Mills theory, known supersymmetric black holes occupy a four-dimensional sheet inside a five-dimensional space of conserved charges. It might seem that exponentially many supersymmetric states exist only near this sheet. This paper proposes a broader picture: a black hole can share charge with supersymmetric excitations outside its horizon, producing large entropy away from the single-black-hole locus.
The five charges are three electric or R-charges \(Q_1,Q_2,Q_3\) and two angular momenta \(J_1,J_2\). Their gravitational setting is type IIB theory on \(AdS_5\times S^5\). The analysis concerns the leading large-\(N\) entropy, with charges of order \(N^2\). It uses known black-hole thermodynamics and motivated conjectures to predict where different kinds of supersymmetric states dominate.
The paper distinguishes an ordinary degeneracy from the superconformal index. A degeneracy counts states at definite charges. The index instead makes a signed count that combines states along lines in charge space. The direction of these lines is equation (8):
\[
t_{I}=\frac{1}{2}\left(1,1,1,-1,-1\right).
\]
Moving along this direction increases the three electric charges while reducing the two angular momenta, without changing the charge combinations resolved by the index. Consequently, an index coefficient cannot automatically be interpreted as the number of states at one particular point. Even where an index line intersects the black hole sheet, other points along it may contain more states.
This observation motivates the two separate questions addressed in the paper: what is the entropy at specified values of all five charges, and which contribution survives as the leading term after taking the signed sum along an index line? The proposed answers rely on different conjectures and carry different levels of evidence.

title: Supersymmetric Grey Galaxies, Dual Dressed Black Holes and the Superconformal Index
text:
Construction and results
The first ingredient is a black hole dressed by supersymmetric excitations. Grey galaxies place angular momentum in a distant gas of high-spin gravitons. Dual dressed black holes place electric charge in dual giant gravitons. Revolving black holes, related to supersymmetric descendants, can share the leading thermodynamics of grey galaxies. The gas or dressing carries a substantial fraction of the charge, while the black-hole core supplies the leading entropy.
The charge decomposition is equation (9):
\[
Z_{i}=Z_{i}^{BH}+Z_{i}^{gas},
\]
Here \(Z_i\) denotes the five charges collectively. The core charges lie on the black hole sheet, while the macroscopic gas charges are nonnegative. At leading order, the proposed components can be treated as noninteracting for the purpose of adding charges and evaluating entropy. The dressed concentration conjecture then prescribes the maximization in equation (10):
\[
\max_{Z_{i}^{\prime}}S_{BH}(Z_{i}^{\prime}),~~~(Z_{i}^{\prime}\leq Z_{i}~~~\forall i=1\ldots 5)
\]
The optimization ranges over allowed black-hole cores. Rather than restricting large entropy to a thin sheet, it extends that entropy into the surrounding charge space. An algorithm identifies the optimal core and which charge components reside in the dressing. The resulting microcanonical ground-state diagram has eleven phases: the pure black-hole phase, three grey-galaxy phases, and seven dual-dressed phases.



Original Figure 2: A schematic slice of the black hole sheet organizes the possible cores. Blue equal-charge surfaces distinguish dual-dressed phases, while the red equal-angular-momentum surface organizes grey-galaxy phases. Reproduced from the paper.


The rank labels count the independent rotation planes occupied by the dressing. A rank-two dual dressed phase carries one electric-charge component outside the core; rank four carries two; rank six carries three. Equal-charge surfaces determine where these possibilities meet. Similarly, grey galaxies distinguish dressing in one or both angular-momentum planes. These are different outcomes of the same constrained entropy problem, rather than separate assumptions about unrelated solutions.
For reference, the known core black holes satisfy the nonlinear density relation in equation (43), with lowercase charges normalized by \(N^2\):
\[
\displaystyle\frac{j_{1}j_{2}}{2}+q_{1}q_{2}q_{3}=\left(q_{1}+q_{2}+q_{3}+\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(q_{1}q_{2}+q_{1}q_{3}+q_{2}q_{3}-\frac{1}{2}(j_{1}+j_{2})\right),
\]
The second ingredient, the unobstructed saddle conjecture, addresses the index. It assumes that the alternating signs do not suppress the leading exponential contribution selected by the largest supersymmetric entropy along an index line. Combining this assumption with the first maximization predicts nine index phases. One is dominated by the ordinary intersection black hole; the other eight are dominated by grey-galaxy or dual-dressed configurations. Thus agreement between the index and the intersection black hole is expected only in part of charge space.

title: Supersymmetric Grey Galaxies, Dual Dressed Black Holes and the Superconformal Index
text:
Interpretation and limits



Original Figure 1: At \(N=10\) on the charge slice specified in the paper, red dots show the numerically evaluated index entropy. Blue curves give the intersection-black-hole prediction; the orange segment gives the grey-galaxy prediction. The comparison is qualitative evidence for the conjectured change of phase. Reproduced from the paper.


The numerical comparison is an independent check using the field-theory index at \(N\leq10\). On a selected charge slice, the data follow the expected departure from the naive black-hole curve toward a grey-galaxy contribution. The choice of slice matters: finite-\(N\) graviton contributions can obscure the leading black-hole physics, and some other comparisons are much less discriminating. Qualitative agreement at these ranks does not establish the asymptotic conjectures for arbitrary charges.
The two conjectures should also remain distinct. Evidence for supersymmetric dressing includes descendant states, probe-brane constructions, and directly enumerated field-theory states. The claim that phase cancellations leave the maximal entropy intact is more tentative. Alternating sums can undergo exponentially strong cancellation, so the second claim does not follow from entropy maximization alone. The paper explicitly discusses circumstances in which such a conjecture could fail.
The analysis additionally assumes that the known family exhausts the relevant single-center supersymmetric black holes. Additional families could change the optimization and detailed phase boundaries. Exact backreacted dressed solutions, higher-rank index computations, and broader charge-space tests remain important checks. Subject to these qualifications, the work gives a concrete alternative to the idea that all extensive supersymmetric entropy is concentrated on the isolated-black-hole sheet.

title: Dual Dressed Black Holes as the End Point of the Charged Superradiant Instability in N = 4 Yang Mills
text: Skip to main content

title: Dual Dressed Black Holes as the End Point of the Charged Superradiant Instability in N = 4 Yang Mills
text:
Motivation and setup
A black hole in anti-de Sitter space can lose stability when it becomes favorable to transfer charge from its horizon to material outside it. The reflecting asymptotic geometry allows emitted excitations to remain in the system. The question is then thermodynamic as well as dynamical: at fixed total energy and charges, what configuration replaces the unstable black hole? This paper investigates that question in type IIB string theory on \(AdS_5\times S^5\), the gravitational dual of strongly coupled \(\mathcal{N}=4\) Yang–Mills theory.
Earlier descriptions emphasized charged scalar condensates and hairy black holes in a five-dimensional gauged-supergravity truncation. A consistent truncation permits solutions within its retained fields, but does not guarantee stability against all fields of the full theory. The ten-dimensional theory contains an infinite tower of charged excitations. The paper shows that large dual giant gravitons provide an instability channel that is absent from the restricted description. In particular, previously proposed hairy endpoints can themselves discharge into these objects.
A dual giant is a D3-brane expanded into the anti-de Sitter directions while carrying angular momentum on the internal sphere. The proposed endpoint contains a central black hole and one, two, or three very large dual giants. Each giant carries charge of order \(N^2\) and lies at a radial position of order \(\sqrt{N}\) in AdS units. Their large separation makes a weakly interacting composite possible even though the total energy outside the horizon is macroscopic.
The charge and energy bookkeeping is written in equation (43):
\[
\begin{split}
&N_{\rm eff}=N-m\\
&E^{BH}=E^{\rm tot}-\sum_{i=1}^{3}Q_i^D\\
&Q_i^{BH}=Q_i^{\rm tot}-Q_i^D\\
&J_i^{BH}=J_i^{\rm tot}.
\end{split}
\]
Here \(m\) is the number of dual giants, \(Q_i^D\) their charges, and \(N_{\rm eff}\) the five-form flux seen by the central black hole. The small flux reduction is important for selecting how many giants occur, even though it is subleading in the leading large-\(N\) thermodynamics.



Original Figure 1 from the paper: fixed-charge paths through the zero-angular-momentum phase diagram. All original panels are retained. The number of intermediate dressing phases depends on charge degeneracies.

title: Dual Dressed Black Holes as the End Point of the Charged Superradiant Instability in N = 4 Yang Mills
text:
Construction and main results
The dominant entropy comes from the core horizon. Its dependence on the remaining energy, charges, angular momenta, and effective flux is summarized in equation (44):
\[
S_{BH}=N_{\rm eff}^{2}\,s_{BH}\left(\frac{E^{BH}}{N_{\rm eff}^{2}},\frac{Q_i^{BH}}{N_{\rm eff}^{2}},\frac{J_j^{BH}}{N_{\rm eff}^{2}}\right).
\]
At fixed total charges, the preferred division between core and dressing maximizes this entropy. The leading derivative, equation (48), takes a particularly transparent form:
\[
\frac{\partial S_{BH}}{\partial Q_i^D}=\beta(\mu_i-1),\qquad Q^{BH}<Q^{\rm tot}.
\]
The inverse temperature is \(\beta\), and \(\mu_i\) is the core chemical potential. If a potential exceeds unity, moving the corresponding charge into a dual giant increases entropy. An interior equilibrium therefore pins that potential to unity. Channels in which no giant is present instead satisfy the appropriate endpoint condition with potential below unity. Depending on how many channels are occupied, the resulting dual dressed black holes have rank two, four, or six.
The leading entropy does not determine the number of giants by itself. At the next order, the loss of effective flux reduces the central entropy. Within the proposed family, this favors the smallest number of giants needed to carry the dressing: one, two, or three in the respective phases. The paper analyzes both unequal-charge nonrotating configurations and equal-charge rotating configurations, displaying phase boundaries and competition with rotationally dressed grey galaxies.
The canonical description reaches the same threshold from another direction. A dual giant becomes macroscopically occupied when a chemical potential approaches unity closely enough. Equation (56) gives the relevant large-\(N\) scaling:
\[
\mu_i=1-\frac{\chi_i}{N^2}.
\]
The paper also studies the quantum mechanics of a giant near the black hole, including potential tunneling into the horizon. The threshold picked by that analysis agrees with the thermodynamic equilibrium condition. Approximate ten-dimensional solutions incorporate the gravitational backreaction of the large giants: their contribution to the asymptotic charges is significant, while the metric perturbation can still be handled linearly in the appropriate large-\(N\) regime.



Original Figure 5 from the paper: an equal-charge slice with \(J_1=J_2=2\). The colored threshold curves distinguish charged and rotational dressing and show how a dressed state’s entropy is assigned from its core.

title: Dual Dressed Black Holes as the End Point of the Charged Superradiant Instability in N = 4 Yang Mills
text:
Interpretation and limits
The main physical lesson is that a black hole need not store all of a state’s conserved charges behind its horizon. A relatively simple core can coexist with distant objects carrying a substantial share of the charge. Holographically, this enlarges the candidate equilibrium phases of a familiar gauge theory. It also shows why a solution stable inside a consistent truncation may fail to describe equilibrium in the full string-theory spectrum.
The proposed phase dominance is a conjecture supported by the construction and thermodynamic analysis, rather than a proof excluding every possible state. The approximation uses large \(N\), strong coupling, a small number of widely separated dual giants, and controlled inverse-\(N\) corrections. The paper explicitly leaves open the possibility of other nonlinear solutions with greater entropy. Stability against the analyzed tunneling channel does not by itself establish stability against all conceivable perturbations.
The displayed phase diagrams also omit Gregory–Laflamme instabilities and the associated black holes localized in ten dimensions. Their proposed interpretation is therefore restricted to regimes where the participating five-dimensional cores are stable against that effect. Completing the full charge-and-angular-momentum phase diagram, understanding the corresponding microscopic states, and constructing more general nonlinear dressed solutions remain further tasks. These qualifications preserve the distinction between the explicit approximate solutions and the broader equilibrium picture they motivate.

title: Towards a Classification of Holographic Multi-partite Entanglement Measures

title: Towards a Classification of Holographic Multi-partite Entanglement Measures
text:
Looking beyond one entanglement surface
In holography, ordinary entanglement entropy connects a boundary quantum state to the area of a minimal surface in a gravitational spacetime. That connection is powerful, but it begins with a division into only two parties. A state split among several regions has many additional patterns of correlation. This paper develops a framework for asking which multipartite quantities admit similarly useful geometric descriptions and which can probe the original bulk geometry, rather than requiring a completely new gravitational solution.
The difference between probing and backreacting is already present for two parties. A Rényi entropy at a general replica index requires a geometry with a finite conical defect. Taking the appropriate limit removes that defect and gives a minimal-area quantity in the original spacetime. The paper seeks multipartite analogues of this mechanism, starting from local-unitary invariants of a pure state and organizing them into families that admit a suitable continuation.
A general invariant is built by contracting copies of the wavefunction with conjugate copies. Each party contributes a permutation specifying how its indices are paired. This description supports both classification and counting: disconnected contraction diagrams factorize, while connected diagrams supply the basic building blocks. There are rapidly growing numbers of possibilities, so geometric usefulness provides an extra selection principle. In this work, the word “measure” does not imply that positivity or monotonicity under all allowed quantum operations has been established.
A particularly tractable family comes from independent cyclic permutations assigned to the parties. The replica data are expressed using integer labels, and special families interpolate toward a probe limit. This construction extends the earlier multi-entropy and allows different pieces of the eventual bulk network to carry different weights. It turns the search for one privileged multipartite number into a structured collection of boundary observables.



Original Figure 12, complete figure. The chamber decomposition ties each wall to the relative permutation of its neighboring parties. Source figure.

title: Towards a Classification of Holographic Multi-partite Entanglement Measures
section: The replica construction and its weighted geometric answer
text:
The replica construction and its weighted geometric answer
To compute these quantities in a field theory, copies of a Euclidean path integral are glued according to their permutations. The resulting replicated boundary is filled by a gravitational saddle. The decisive assumption is that its dominant filling preserves the boundary replica symmetry. When it does, the bulk can be quotiented to a simpler geometry containing conical singularities, with each singular segment associated with a boundary-region interface.
Original equation (34) writes the corresponding cosmic-brane contribution:
\[
\displaystyle{\mathcal{S}}_{\rm br}^{(k)}=\frac{k-1}{4kG_{N}}\int dy^{D-1}\sqrt{h}=\frac{k-1}{4kG_{N}}A
\tag{34}
\]
The cone order sets the brane tension, the induced metric measures its worldvolume, and the area factor makes the geometric content explicit. Continuing toward the probe limit sends the backreaction away. A network of weighted minimal surfaces then remains in the unreplicated geometry. Figure 12 shows the boundary regions and the corresponding bulk chambers, whose separating walls form the web.
The weighted minimization defining the area functional appears in original equation (36):
\[
\displaystyle\partial_{n}{\mathcal{S}}_{\rm grav}|_{n=1}=\frac{1}{4G_{N}}{\rm min}_{\cal W}\left\{\sum_{\widetilde{L}_{\sigma_{\mathtt{a}}^{-1}\sigma_{\mathtt{b}}}\in{\mathcal{W}}}\log({\rm lcm}(m_{\mathtt{a}},m_{\mathtt{b}}))A_{{\mathtt{a}},{\mathtt{b}}}\right\}\equiv\frac{1}{4G_{N}}A_{\rm min}^{\cal W}.
\tag{36}
\]
Here the weights are logarithms of least common multiples of the integer party labels. They are fixed by the replica construction rather than chosen by hand. Minimization includes the allowed arrangement of the web, not merely the position of one preselected junction. The resulting probe measure has the compact form of original equation (37):
\[
\displaystyle S^{\{m_{\mathtt{a}}\}}=\frac{1}{4G_{N}}A_{\rm min}^{\cal W}.
\tag{37}
\]
This is the multipartite geometric prescription: a weighted area divided by the gravitational coupling. In three bulk dimensions, the areas reduce to lengths of geodesic segments. As an explicit example, the equal-label three-party case reduces to a junction problem. Original equation (43) gives:
\[
\displaystyle S^{\{m,m,m\}}=\frac{\log m}{4G_{N}}{\rm min}_{X}\Big(\sum_{i}\ell(P_{i},X))\Big).
\tag{43}
\]
The boundary endpoints are fixed while the interior junction is optimized. Unequal labels generalize the competition among the segments. This makes the geometric meaning of the boundary family concrete: changing the observable changes the web’s tensions and therefore which portions of spacetime it probes.
The paper tests the proposal against two-dimensional CFT calculations involving twist-operator correlation functions and semiclassical conformal blocks. The nontrivial dependence on boundary positions, including cross-ratio dependence, agrees in the cases analyzed. The tests also identify a limitation: parts of the overall normalization depend on twist three-point coefficients that are not fully fixed by the conformal-block calculation. The evidence therefore supports a detailed prescription within its assumptions without replacing those assumptions with a universal theorem.

title: Towards a Classification of Holographic Multi-partite Entanglement Measures
section: Finer bulk partitions, with assumptions kept visible
text:
Finer bulk partitions, with assumptions kept visible
Different choices of multipartite measure can draw different webs across the same spacetime. Overlaying them partitions a bulk slice more finely than a single bipartite entanglement wedge does. Figure 24 displays this idea using only the paper’s original construction. Regions inaccessible to one boundary party can be subdivided by observables sensitive to several parties together, motivating questions about a more detailed account of bulk locality.



Original Figure 24, complete figure. Several probe webs refine the bulk partition associated with a fixed boundary decomposition. Source figure.


The paper discusses a possible connection to quantum error correction: finer geometric partitions might encode distinctions between which combinations of boundary regions can reconstruct bulk information. This is a motivation and prospective application, not a demonstrated multipartite reconstruction theorem. It suggests what further information-theoretic properties would be valuable to establish for the new observables.
Two technical qualifications are especially important. First, continuation away from integer replica data must be defined with care. The discussion explains that uniqueness and existence are nontrivial; a simple continuation for generalized GHZ states does not automatically satisfy standard sufficient growth conditions. Second, boundary replica symmetry can be broken by the dominant bulk filling. A three-party example at replica index three illustrates that failure, while a four-party example at index two admits an explicitly symmetric filling.
These limitations motivate the later study of bulk replica symmetry rather than invalidating the framework’s useful cases. The outcome is a broad construction of candidate probes, a conditional gravitational derivation, explicit CFT tests, and a clear set of questions about continuation, saddle dominance, quantum corrections, and operational entanglement properties. Its main achievement is to make the multipartite geometry systematic enough that these questions can be asked precisely.

title: Everyday Radio Telescope
text:
Skip to main content
No journal publication or individual INSPIRE record has been confirmed for this paper. The original arXiv article is the primary source for this summary.

title: Everyday Radio Telescope
text:
Motivation and setup
Radio astronomy offers a way to study astronomical objects beyond visible light, but the equipment can appear inaccessible to an undergraduate laboratory or amateur group. This project develops an affordable experiment from commercially available satellite-television components. Its aim is educational as well as observational: to connect receiving electronics, digitization, calibration, statistical noise, and astronomical interpretation in a working instrument.
The telescope operates near 11.2 GHz. A parabolic dish concentrates incoming radiation onto a low-noise block receiver, or LNB. A satellite finder acts as a square-law detector, producing a signal related to received intensity. An Arduino Uno digitizes the output with a ten-bit analog-to-digital converter at ten samples per second. A set-top box supplies power, and a Python pipeline records and displays the measurements. The instrument is an intensity-measuring system; the paper does not present it as an imaging array or a frequency-resolving radio spectrometer.



Original Figure 1 from the paper: the instrument’s signal and acquisition chain.


The Sun supplies a strong first target. Geostationary satellites provide reference signals for calibration, and sky observations away from a target supply the background. Pointing is manual, using predicted altitude and azimuth. For satellite calibration, rotating the LNB aligns its receiving element with the transmitted polarization and maximizes the detected signal. This makes the polarization response part of the experiment rather than an invisible correction.
The calibration begins with the Friis transmission relation, reproduced from equation (2):
\[
\frac{P_r}{P_t}=G_tG_r\left(\frac{\lambda}{4\pi R}\right)^2.
\]
Here the received and transmitted powers are \(P_r\) and \(P_t\), the antenna gains are \(G_r\) and \(G_t\), \(R\) is the satellite distance, and \(\lambda\) is the observing wavelength. Satellite equivalent isotropically radiated power combines the transmitter power and gain, allowing the received reference power to be estimated from accessible satellite information.

title: Everyday Radio Telescope
text:
Construction and main results
Converting a voltage change into an astronomical measurement requires both the detector calibration and an estimate of the effective collecting area. The receiving gain is related to dish diameter and aperture efficiency by equation (4):
\[
G_r=\eta_A\left(\frac{\pi d}{\lambda}\right)^2.
\]
The aperture efficiency \(\eta_A\) accounts for the difference between geometric dish area and effective collecting area. The appendix uses this information to turn the measured satellite voltage above background into a power scale. The solar signal is then calibrated relative to the satellite observation, preferably taken close in time so that instrumental conditions are comparable.
A drift scan holds the antenna pointing fixed while the sky moves through its beam. Fitting the solar transit with a Gaussian provides a beam-width estimate as well as a recognizable source detection. The paper reports beam widths of approximately \(3.4\)–\(3.5\) degrees, with the tabulated fits giving \(3.357\pm0.021\) and \(3.501\pm0.007\) degrees. These measurements agree with the approximate beam width expected for the instrument. The broad beam makes source acquisition forgiving, while also limiting angular resolution.



Original Figure 4 from the paper: solar transit data and its Gaussian fit. The plotted measurements and fitted curve are reproduced directly from the article.


The appendix next converts received power to flux density, including the single-polarization response and the difference between the satellite’s transmitted bandwidth and the receiver’s solar-observation bandwidth. Dividing the flux by the solar solid angle gives intensity. Assuming thermal radiation in the Rayleigh–Jeans regime, the final temperature relation shown in Appendix A, unnumbered, is
\[
T=\frac{I\lambda^2}{2K_B}=10078\,K.
\]
This is the paper’s worked calibration example, with \(I\) the inferred intensity and \(K_B\) Boltzmann’s constant. The two reported solar brightness temperatures are 10078 K and 10136 K, with quoted uncertainties of 295 K and 324 K. Brightness temperature describes the observed intensity at the operating frequency; it should not be confused with a direct measurement of the Sun’s photospheric temperature.
Sensitivity can improve by averaging longer. The relevant relation is the radiometer equation, equation (1):
\[
\sigma_T\propto\frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau\Delta\nu_{RF}}}.
\]
The output fluctuation \(\sigma_T\) decreases as integration time \(\tau\) or receiver bandwidth \(\Delta\nu_{RF}\) increases, under the assumptions behind that noise model. Increasing integration from one second to sixty seconds enabled the reported drift-scan detections of Saturn and a Galactic-arm crossing. The Saturn detection has a reported signal-to-noise ratio of three, with transit timing checked against the predicted sky motion.

title: Everyday Radio Telescope
text:
Interpretation and limits
This experiment brings several normally separate classroom topics into one measurement. The receiving chain illustrates amplification and detection; the digitizer turns a continuous voltage into a sampled series; calibration connects the output to physical units; and drift scans connect time-domain structure to the sky. A simple setup can therefore teach the reasoning behind a radio measurement without requiring a large professional observatory.
The paper also investigates noise rather than treating every fluctuation as astronomical. Comparing ordinary sky measurements with observations made while the LNB is shielded helps distinguish system-generated features. Fourier analysis shows instrumental structure in the time series, including a feature around half a hertz. Ambient temperature changes also track the detector voltage: the reported correlation coefficient is 0.98. Longer averaging alone cannot remove a drifting calibration or establish that every feature comes from a celestial source.
The reported weaker-source detections should be read with those limitations in mind. Their interpretation relies on timing, pointing, background behavior, and modest signal-to-noise, rather than high-resolution imaging. The solar calibration assumes thermal emission, an aperture efficiency, published satellite powers, and a linear extrapolation between the satellite and solar bandwidths. Those assumptions explain what the quoted temperature estimates mean and where systematic uncertainty can enter.
There is also a dimensional inconsistency within the original article: the setup description gives a 68 cm dish, whereas the appendix’s numerical gain substitution uses 0.71 m. This summary preserves the source equations and reported measurements without silently harmonizing those inputs. The original paper remains the reference for reproducing the experiment and evaluating its calibration in detail.

title: Research
text:
Quantum Information in Quantum Gravity

From two subsystems to many
Entanglement entropy measures quantum correlations across a division into two parts. In a pure state with three or more subsystems, there are additional ways for correlations to be shared. Grouping parties together can hide this structure: the entropies of individual subsystems need not capture every invariant of the full state. My work develops measures that treat the multiple parties together and asks how their algebraic structure appears in gravity.
The starting point is the replica method. For a bipartite system, copies of a reduced density matrix are joined cyclically, and the resulting contraction gives a Rényi entropy. The multi-entropy construction instead uses a lattice of replicas, with a separate cyclic permutation associated with each party. Its Rényi version is defined in equation (14) of the original paper:
\[
S^{({\mathtt{q}})}_{n}\equiv\frac{1}{1-n}{\rm Log}\,({\mathcal{Z}}_{n}^{({\mathtt{q}})}/({\mathcal{Z}}_{1}^{({\mathtt{q}})})^{n^{{\mathtt{q}}-1}}).
\]
Here \(\mathtt{q}\) counts the parties, \(n\) is the replica parameter, and \(\mathcal{Z}^{(\mathtt{q})}_n\) is the specified contraction of copies of the state and its conjugate. The normalization removes dependence on the norm of the state. The construction reduces to the familiar Rényi entropy for two parties, while retaining information about more general multipartite correlations.



Original Figure 2 from arXiv:2206.09723: graphical notation for the three-party density matrix and the contraction defining \(\mathcal{Z}^{(3)}_4\).


The continuation toward one replica defines multi-entropy itself, as in equation (17) of the same paper:
\[
S^{({\mathtt{q}})}={\rm lim}_{n\to{1}}\,S^{({\mathtt{q}})}_{n}.
\]
Analytic continuation is a substantive part of the prescription. One cannot infer its existence or uniqueness just from the integer-replica definition. A related question is whether these quantities decrease when two parties are merged. Work on the monotonicity conjecture proves particular cases and develops evidence for others, while leaving the general statement conjectural.


Replica symmetry and bulk geometry
In holography, a quantum field theory admits a gravitational description in one higher dimension. Ordinary entanglement entropy is encoded by an extremal area. The multipartite problem suggests a richer structure: networks of surfaces that partition the bulk into chambers, with junctions where surfaces meet. The replica construction determines the gluing of boundary regions; a compatible bulk saddle must implement that gluing geometrically.



Original Figure 12 from arXiv:2304.06082: boundary regions \(\mathcal{R}_{\mathtt a}\), bulk chambers \(\mathcal{C}_{\mathtt a}\), and the walls separating them.


The classification program studies more general permutation contractions and the finite groups organizing their replica symmetries. The subsequent bulk replica symmetry analysis asks when those symmetries can extend to a smooth covering geometry. This constrains which proposed networks admit a symmetric gravitational realization. The goal is to identify the quantum observables and the geometric assumptions required for each correspondence, including the possibility that a dominant saddle breaks replica symmetry.

title: Research
text:
Black Holes and Holography

Which states dominate?
A black hole with specified charges is one possible way to organize the states of a gravitational system. It need not be the configuration with the greatest entropy. In anti-de Sitter space, additional charge or angular momentum can reside outside a central black hole, producing phases that combine a black-hole core with a surrounding gas or condensate. My work investigates when these configurations dominate and how their transitions appear in the dual quantum theory.
Supersymmetry makes this problem more tractable by imposing an energy bound. In the two-charge \(AdS_4\) setting, equation (1) of the ground-state phases paper reads:
\[
E\ell\geq J+2(Q_{1}\ell+Q_{2}\ell)~.
\]
Here \(\ell\) is the AdS radius, \(E\) is energy, \(J\) is angular momentum, and \(Q_1,Q_2\) are electric charges. States saturating this bound are BPS. Regular single-center supersymmetric black holes obey a further nonlinear relation between their charges, so they occupy a restricted surface in charge space. A core-plus-gas configuration can extend the family of candidate ground states beyond that surface.



Original Figure 1 from arXiv:2510.16274: the black-hole sheet, including its folded region. The translucent foreground reveals the second branch.


The charged-superradiance study develops dual dressed black holes as candidate endpoints of an instability in \(AdS_5\). The grey-galaxy and index study connects several dressed phases to the superconformal index. This index is a protected, signed count of states: cancellations mean that its entropy need not simply equal the total number of supersymmetric states. Keeping these two counting problems distinct is essential to understanding the proposed phase diagrams.


Which geometries belong in the sum?
The same question has a Euclidean formulation. A path-integral computation sums over geometries and matter fields. Equation (1) of the complex-black-hole paper expresses the starting point as
\[
\mathcal{Z}=\int\mathcal{D}g_{\mu\nu}\mathcal{D}\Psi\,e^{-I_{E}[g_{\mu\nu},\Psi]}~,
\]
where \(I_E\) is the Euclidean action. The supersymmetric black-hole saddles relevant to the index have complex metrics. Solving the equations of motion therefore leaves an additional question: which complex geometries are admissible in the integral?
The Kontsevich–Segal–Witten criterion tests convergence of auxiliary matter kinetic terms on a complex geometry. In a suitable diagonal basis, its condition is equation (20) of the same paper:
\[
\sum_i|\arg\lambda_i|<\pi~.
\]
The \(\lambda_i\) are the diagonal metric entries in that basis. The test must hold throughout spacetime. For the studied \(AdS_5\) family, analytic asymptotic calculations and numerical bulk checks find agreement between admissibility and the convergence region of the boundary index.



Original Figure 1 from arXiv:2602.05979: imposing the test at every polar angle selects the region bounded by the red curves, matching index convergence.


Failure near the asymptotic boundary is consistent with the appearance of a distant angular-momentum-carrying gas. This provides a diagnostic for a change of phase, without constructing the complete replacement saddle. The criterion also has limits: in the related two-charge \(AdS_4\) setting it misses an instability. Comparing these examples helps distinguish a successful test within one family from a universal rule for gravitational path integrals.

title: A New Multipartite Entanglement Measure and Its Holographic Dual
text: Skip to main content

title: A New Multipartite Entanglement Measure and Its Holographic Dual
text:
Motivation and setup
Entanglement entropy is a powerful bridge between quantum information and geometry. It describes how a pure quantum state is shared between two subsystems. In a holographic theory, the same quantity can be calculated from a surface in the gravitational bulk. A state shared among three or more parties contains additional structure, however: choosing a single division into two groups can hide distinctions between different patterns of multipartite entanglement. This paper asks whether there is a natural, permutation-symmetric extension of entropy that also has a direct geometric description.
The starting point is a pure state in a tensor product of \(\mathtt{q}\) Hilbert spaces. An entanglement quantity must be unchanged by independent unitary changes of basis in each factor. Such invariants can be built by taking copies of the wavefunction and its conjugate, then contracting their indices. In the two-party case, these contractions reduce to products of traces of powers of a reduced density matrix. For more parties, there are many more possible contractions, so extending the familiar entropy requires a specific choice.
The paper selects a family with a regular replica structure. After eliminating redundant relabelings, there are \(n^{\mathtt{q}-1}\) copies arranged on a \((\mathtt{q}-1)\)-dimensional periodic lattice. Each party has its own prescribed cyclic contraction. Although this representation chooses one party to trace out first, the resulting invariant is symmetric under exchange of the original parties. The normalization is included explicitly, so the definition does not depend on an arbitrary norm of the state.
The resulting Rényi multi-entropy is defined in equation (14):
\[
S^{(\mathtt{q})}_{n}\equiv\frac{1}{1-n}{\rm Log}\,\left(\mathcal{Z}_{n}^{(\mathtt{q})}/\left(\mathcal{Z}_{1}^{(\mathtt{q})}\right)^{n^{\mathtt{q}-1}}\right).
\]
Here \(\mathcal{Z}_{n}^{(\mathtt{q})}\) denotes the prescribed replica contraction. Taking the continuation to \(n=1\) defines multi-entropy. With two parties this recovers the ordinary von Neumann entropy; with more parties it probes a different contraction pattern.



Original Figure 2 from the paper: the three-party contraction producing \(\mathcal{Z}_{4}^{(3)}\). The periodic lattice is a replica-index diagram, not a spatial lattice in the underlying theory.

title: A New Multipartite Entanglement Measure and Its Holographic Dual
text:
Construction and main results
A useful check comes from generalized GHZ states, whose basis labels are shared among all parties. The replica contraction can then be evaluated explicitly because a common index runs through the whole network. The resulting multi-entropy, equation (22), is
\[
S^{(\mathtt{q})}=(1-\mathtt{q})\sum_i |\lambda_i|^2\,{\rm log}|\lambda_i|^2.
\]
The coefficients \(\lambda_i\) specify the normalized GHZ state. This example demonstrates both the familiar two-party limit and the extra dependence on the number of parties. It also illustrates why a multipartite quantity can distinguish information that is lost when one examines only selected reduced-state spectra. The paper gives an explicit isospectral example to make that distinction concrete.
For holographic states, the same replica construction becomes a boundary condition for a gravitational path integral. Assuming the relevant replica symmetry extends into the bulk, the replicated geometry can be quotiented by that symmetry. Fixed loci become conical defects, represented in the calculation by cosmic branes. In the multipartite construction several such loci can meet, producing a connected web rather than a single separating surface.
The gravitational action near these defects determines the leading answer. The paper checks possible extra contributions at junctions by excising small tubular neighborhoods and examining the corner terms. In Einstein gravity, those junction contributions vanish as the neighborhood shrinks. Near \(n=1\), the brane tension vanishes, and the web can therefore be found as an area-minimizing probe configuration in the original geometry.
This gives the central classical prescription, equation (30):
\[
S^{(\mathtt{q})}=\frac{A(\mathcal{W})}{4G_N}.
\]
The web \(\mathcal{W}\) must end on the boundaries of the specified regions and contain subwebs homologous to each region. These conditions matter: a small area alone is insufficient if the web does not implement the required partition. The resulting geometry resembles a soap film attached to a wire frame, which motivates the name “soap-film prescription.”



Original Figure 3 from the paper: the local junction used to analyze gravitational corner terms. This diagram supports the junction calculation; it is not a newly drawn example of a complete bulk solution.

title: A New Multipartite Entanglement Measure and Its Holographic Dual
text:
Interpretation and limits
The result extends the geometric dictionary of holography from one bipartition to a symmetric many-party observable. A network with junctions can encode how several regions share a state, whereas a single minimal surface describes one division. The construction also makes contact with ordinary soap-film junction rules in a spatial slice, supplying a geometric way to think about the new boundary quantity.
Several qualifications are essential. The classical argument uses Einstein gravity and assumes an appropriate replica-symmetric bulk saddle. The analytic continuation away from integer replica number is another substantive issue. The paper does not establish its existence and uniqueness for arbitrary finite-dimensional states; it restricts its definition to cases with a manifest continuation, including the holographic construction under consideration. Higher-derivative gravity can introduce additional junction contributions and needs a separate treatment.
The quantum extension is explicitly a conjecture. The proposed quantum extremal soap film extremizes the combination in equation (32):
\[
\frac{A(\mathcal{W})}{4G_N}+S_{\rm bulk}^{(\mathtt{q})}(\mathcal{W}).
\]
The second term is the bulk multi-entropy of the regions separated by the web. Its inclusion parallels quantum corrections to ordinary holographic entropy, but the paper does not promote that analogy into an unconditional proof. A covariant extension using extremal webs is also proposed. These questions provide the motivation for studying more general invariant constructions and their replica symmetries in subsequent work.

title: Monotonicity Conjecture for Multi-party Entanglement I
text: Skip to main content

title: Monotonicity Conjecture for Multi-party Entanglement I
section: What should happen when two parties become one?
text:
What should happen when two parties become one?
A multipartite quantum state can be viewed at different resolutions. Four laboratories may be treated separately, or two may be grouped into a single laboratory. The underlying state does not change, but the distinction between correlations inside a party and correlations between parties does. A measure intended to capture multipartite entanglement should respond meaningfully to this change of perspective. This paper investigates the proposal that a family of measures should not increase when parties are merged: monotonicity under coarse graining.
The proposal concerns pure states and a family called Rényi multi-entropies. It complements local-unitary invariance, symmetry between parties, and additivity for independent product states. Original equation (6) expresses the desired ordering for a general family of measures:
\[
\displaystyle{\cal M}^{({\mathtt{q}})}(|\Psi\rangle)-{\cal M}^{({\mathtt{q}}-1)}(|\Psi_{[A_{\mathtt{a}}A_{\mathtt{b}}]}\rangle)\geq 0\qquad\quad\forall\,{\mathtt{a}},{\mathtt{b}}.
\tag{6}
\]
The bracketed subscript means that two Hilbert-space factors are now regarded as one party. Repeated mergers generate many inequalities, organized by the partial order of partitions of the original parties. Thus the conjecture is a hierarchy rather than a single three-party comparison. An inequality for one merger can constrain every route through which a finely partitioned system is reduced to a coarser description.
The distinction from ordinary monotonicity under local operations and classical communication is central. The paper does not establish that the measures are mixed-state entanglement monotones under such operations. Instead, it asks a separate, mathematically concrete question about pure-state measures at different party resolutions. Treating coarse graining as a relabeling of tensor factors also makes clear that no physical loss of the total state is required for the proposed inequality to have content.

title: Monotonicity Conjecture for Multi-party Entanglement I
section: Replica lattices and several routes to evidence
text:
Replica lattices and several routes to evidence
The construction begins with a polynomial local-unitary invariant: copies of the wavefunction and its complex conjugate are contracted with permutation-defined patterns. For Rényi multi-entropy the permutations are lattice translations, and the contraction can be drawn as a periodic lattice. Figure 3 shows a connected component of the three-party example. Its directions represent different parties, so identifying parties changes the contraction geometry in a controlled way.



Original Figure 3, complete figure. One connected component of the invariant built from three independent cyclic generators. Source figure.


The Rényi multi-entropy is a logarithm of that invariant with a normalization depending on the number of parties. Original equation (11) defines it:
\[
\displaystyle S_{n}^{({\mathtt{q}})}:=\frac{1}{1-n}\frac{1}{n^{{\mathtt{q}}-2}}{\rm log}({\cal E}_{n}^{({\mathtt{q}})}).
\tag{11}
\]
This normalization is necessary when comparing descriptions with different numbers of parties. The paper translates the entropy statement into an inequality between polynomial invariants, so the conjecture can be tested without presuming a general positivity theorem for the logarithm’s argument. For pure states the equivalent formulation is original equation (13):
\[
\displaystyle{S}_{n}^{({\mathtt{q}})}(|\psi\rangle)\geq{S}_{n}^{({\mathtt{q}}-1)}(|\psi_{[A_{\mathtt{a}}A_{\mathtt{b}}]}\rangle)\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad{\cal E}_{n}^{({\mathtt{q}})}(|\psi\rangle)\leq\Big({\cal E}_{n}^{({\mathtt{q}}-1)}(|\psi_{[A_{\mathtt{a}}A_{\mathtt{b}}]}\rangle)\Big)^{n}.
\tag{13}
\]
Several complementary calculations then probe this assertion. Perturbation theory around factorized density matrices verifies it to second order, where the comparison reduces to controlled quadratic expressions. For classical probability distributions, regarded as diagonal density matrices of a purification, the proof uses inequalities between positive coefficients. Generalized three-party W states give another analytic test with genuinely quantum correlations. In that example the replica contraction can be reorganized as a lattice problem and related to a dimer model.



Original Figure 8, complete figure. Resolving the density matrix is a step toward the lattice and dimer representation used in the analytic W-state check. Source figure.


The calculations are supplemented by numerical tests of randomly selected finite-dimensional states with several party numbers, dimensions, and replica indices. Agreement across these examples is evidence for the conjecture, while each analytic argument has its stated domain. The variety matters: diagonal states, small perturbations, W states, and random states probe different aspects of the same contraction inequality rather than repeating one special calculation.

title: Monotonicity Conjecture for Multi-party Entanglement I
text:
Evidence, saturation, and open questions
A holographic argument supplies a geometrical perspective at replica index two. Under the brane-web prescription, merging parties removes interfaces between the corresponding bulk chambers. The cone parameter on an interface is continuously reduced until that singular segment disappears. The gravitational action responds according to a Schläfli-type formula. The action derivative used in the discussion is original equation (101):
\[
\displaystyle\partial_{n}S({\widetilde{\cal B}}_{n}^{({\mathtt{2}})})=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\frac{1}{4G_{N}}A({\cal W}).
\tag{101}
\]
Its positive-area right-hand side controls the direction of change. The method connects an information-theoretic inequality to the response of a hyperbolic cone geometry, provided the relevant saddle and continuation satisfy the geometric assumptions.
The main claim remains a conjecture for general multipartite quantum states. The paper proves particular classes and perturbative cases, gives a holographic argument in its specified setting, and reports extensive numerical checks. These do not amount to a universal proof. In particular, the analysis does not establish positivity of every polynomial invariant, and it explicitly leaves that question open. Expressing the conjecture directly as an invariant inequality keeps this limitation visible.
The holographic argument likewise uses more than local-unitary invariance. It relies on a replica-symmetric bulk description and the ability to vary cone parameters along a family of geometries. Boundary replica symmetry need not always survive in the dominant bulk saddle. The paper’s discussion focuses on two-dimensional holographic theories and replica index two, where the cited construction supports the brane-web prescription. It does not extend the argument indiscriminately to arbitrary replica indices or dimensions.
Saturation offers another avenue for understanding the result. For some states, grouping particular parties leaves the measure unchanged. The paper relates such behavior to the absence of relevant correlations and asks whether multipartite analogues of mutual information can sharpen that interpretation. Possible mixed-state extensions through convex-roof constructions and connections to quantum error correction are future directions, rather than established consequences of the tests. The contribution is a precise candidate ordering principle together with several independent ways to investigate it.

title: Multi-invariants and Bulk Replica Symmetry
text: Skip to main content

title: Multi-invariants and Bulk Replica Symmetry
section: The question: when does boundary symmetry survive in gravity?
text:
The question: when does boundary symmetry survive in gravity?
Entanglement between several parts of a quantum system contains information that cannot be captured by examining just one division into two parts. A natural starting point is to construct quantities unchanged by independent changes of basis in each part. This paper calls these quantities multi-invariants. It studies polynomial invariants obtained by contracting copies of a wavefunction with copies of its complex conjugate, with a separate contraction pattern for each party. Permutations record those patterns, turning a potentially complicated tensor expression into a precise combinatorial object.
The physical setting is the vacuum of a two-dimensional holographic conformal field theory: a theory with large central charge and a suitable gap that admits a semiclassical gravitational description. Dividing the spatial circle into party regions makes its vacuum a multipartite state. Each contraction becomes an instruction for gluing copies of the Euclidean path integral. The resulting replicated surface can have handles and branch points. Evaluating its partition function computes the invariant, with normalization removing the original state’s norm.
The central question is whether this complicated replicated problem has a simpler description using a single copy of the boundary. The normalized invariant removes its overall replica multiplicity, as in original equation (7):
\[
\displaystyle\tilde{\mathcal{E}}\equiv{\mathcal{E}}^{1/{n_{r}}},
\tag{7}
\]
Here the replica number counts copies of the wavefunction. When a replica symmetry acts freely and transitively on the copies, quotienting the replicated boundary returns the original sphere. To do the same in gravity, however, the dominant bulk filling must preserve that symmetry. Symmetry of the boundary data alone does not guarantee symmetry of the dominant gravitational saddle. Establishing when this additional step is justified is the purpose of the paper.



Original Figure 7, all panels. Different free normal subgroups give different intermediate handlebodies but the same final orbifold. Source figure.

title: Multi-invariants and Bulk Replica Symmetry
section: From replicated surfaces to hyperbolic orbifolds
text:
From replicated surfaces to hyperbolic orbifolds
With an unbroken bulk replica symmetry, the invariant is determined by the difference between the orbifold action and the unreplicated action. Original equation (22) is:
\[
\displaystyle\tilde{\mathcal{E}}=e^{-S_{\rm grav}[\hat{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{E}}]+S_{\rm grav}[{\mathcal{B}}]}.
\tag{22}
\]
The quotient geometry generally contains conical singularities: lines around which a full circuit covers less angle than in smooth space. In three-dimensional Euclidean gravity these geometries can be described using discrete groups of hyperbolic isometries, called Kleinian groups. Their algebra records how the replicated boundary and its bulk filling fit together. Reflection symmetries extend the construction and connect it to Coxeter groups, which are generated by reflections satisfying pairwise relations.
Figure 7 captures a striking consequence. One Kleinian group can contain different free normal subgroups. Quotienting by one such subgroup first gives a handlebody, and a further finite quotient produces the final orbifold. Different choices can change the genus and the replica presentation while leaving that orbifold unchanged. Consequently, infinitely large families of normalized invariants agree on the holographic vacuum at the semiclassical level. These are special equalities of holographic observables; they are not identities for every quantum state.
The classification also has a local geometric face. Singular lines meet at junctions constrained by which finite groups can act around a point. The allowed three-line junctions are associated with the four families listed in original equation (29):
\[
\displaystyle(m_{12},m_{23},m_{31})=\quad(2,2,n),\quad(2,3,3),\quad(2,3,4),\quad(2,3,5).
\tag{29}
\]
The integers determine cone angles, and therefore encode differing effective cosmic-brane tensions. The complete Figure 10 below displays the associated junctions. These are the paper’s original geometries rather than illustrative networks chosen independently for the website.



Original Figure 10, all four junctions. The labels specify conical angles and distinguish the allowed local group actions. Source figure.


Combining groups along shared subgroups builds more extensive singular networks. This construction separates invariants that preserve bulk replica symmetry only in some configurations of boundary regions from those that do so for every configuration. Requiring preservation throughout the configuration space is highly restrictive: the resulting extended replica groups are finite Coxeter groups. Their defining presentation appears in original equation (10):
\[
\langle r_{1},\cdots r_{{\mathtt{q}}}|(r_{i}r_{j})^{m_{ij}}=e\rangle,\quad m_{ii}=1,\quad m_{ij}=m_{ji}\geq 2
\tag{10}
\]

title: Multi-invariants and Bulk Replica Symmetry
section: What the classification establishes—and where it stops
text:
What the classification establishes—and where it stops
The result explains why a convenient geometric formula is available for some multipartite observables and fails for others. A contraction pattern specifies the boundary replica problem, while the group-theoretic classification decides which patterns admit the required symmetric gravitational filling as regions move. The same analysis supplies families of bulk geometries and relations among their regulated actions. Direct CFT calculations, using covering maps and their accompanying Liouville actions, check selected predictions independently of the bulk quotient construction.
Replica symmetry breaking remains physically meaningful. A symmetric filling can exist without dominating the path integral, so existence alone cannot justify the simplified prescription. The paper discusses cases in which symmetric solutions are subleading and involve Euclidean wormholes with two boundary components. These examples make the distinction between a candidate saddle and the saddle that computes the observable essential.
The scope is also specific: the detailed classification concerns vacuum states of two-dimensional holographic CFTs and their three-dimensional semiclassical bulk duals. Extending the conclusions to arbitrary states, higher dimensions, or finite-central-charge corrections requires further work. Local-unitary invariance likewise does not by itself establish the stronger operational properties of an entanglement monotone. The paper deliberately studies a geometric classification of invariants without claiming that every member satisfies all quantum-information requirements.

title: Phases of Supersymmetric Ground States in AdS₄
text:
Motivation and setup
Supersymmetry places a lower bound on the energy of a state with specified charges. States that saturate it are BPS states, the supersymmetric ground states in their charge sector. Black holes account for enormous numbers of such states, yet familiar regular BPS black holes do not exist at every allowed charge. This work asks what fills the rest of the phase diagram, and how these additional states affect the protected count called the superconformal index.
The setting is supergravity on \(AdS_4\times S^7\), restricted to four electric charges equal in pairs. There are consequently two independent electric charges, \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\), and one angular momentum, \(J\). The BPS energy bound is equation (1):
\[
E\ell\geq J+2(Q_{1}\ell+Q_{2}\ell)~.
\]
Here \(\ell\) is the AdS radius. Saturating this linear inequality is necessary for supersymmetry, but a regular single black hole must also obey a nonlinear charge relation. After rescaling charges by the large-\(N\) parameter \(k=\ell^2/(2G)\), the paper uses densities \(q_1,q_2,j\), their sum \(q\), and difference \(\tilde q\). The nonlinear relation becomes the “black hole sheet,” equation (44):
\[
\displaystyle j=j_{c}(q,\tilde{q})=q\left(\sqrt{1+4\left(q^{2}-\tilde{q}^{2}\right)}-1\right)~.
\]
This sheet is a surface in a three-dimensional charge space. It does not fill the physical region. Its geometry therefore exposes the central puzzle: generic supersymmetric charge sectors cannot be described by an isolated member of the known black-hole family. The paper proposes that they instead contain a black-hole core accompanied by another component carrying the remaining charge.



Original Figure 1: Regular single-component BPS black holes occupy the green sheet, rather than the full three-dimensional charge space. The foreground is translucent so that the folded branch remains visible. Reproduced from the paper.

title: Phases of Supersymmetric Ground States in AdS₄
text:
Construction and results
The construction assumes a two-component system whose energy and charges add at leading order. One component is a BPS black hole; the other is termed a gas. The gas carries macroscopic charge but negligible leading entropy, so the total entropy comes from the core. This is a thermodynamic prescription supported by related constructions, rather than an explicit construction of every proposed supersymmetric geometry.
Given total charges, the allowed cores lie on the black hole sheet and must leave nonnegative charges for the gas. The dominant candidate is found by maximizing the core entropy over that allowed set. On the sheet, the entropy density takes the simple form in equation (45):
\[
s_{BH}(j,q)=\pi\frac{j}{q}~.
\]
This constrained optimization produces distinct phases. On the overrotating side, called Region I, the entropy is greatest when the core retains all electric charge and the gas carries the excess angular momentum. This has the character of a grey galaxy, with angular momentum stored far from the central black hole.
On the overcharged side, Region II, the optimum places all angular momentum in the core while the gas carries electric charge. There are two cases. In Region IIa the core can reach equal electric charges, and the gas absorbs the charge imbalance. In Region IIb the positivity constraints prevent that equal-charge core; the optimum instead has gas carrying only one of the two electric charges. These charged configurations are motivated by dual giant gravitons, with an \(M2\)-brane interpretation in this compactification.
The superconformal index introduces another optimization. Because its chemical potentials obey a supersymmetric constraint, it resolves combinations of charges rather than all three charges independently. In the paper’s density variables, an index line has fixed \(\zeta=q+j\) and \(\tilde\zeta=\tilde q\). Each physical line intersects the black hole sheet once, but this intersection need not supply its largest entropy.
Assuming that cancellations in the signed index do not remove the leading entropy maximum, the paper compares configurations along each line. For nonnegative \(\tilde\zeta\), its result is equation (126):
\[
s_{\mathcal{I}}(\zeta,\tilde{\zeta})=\begin{cases}s_{X}(\zeta,\tilde{\zeta})&,~~{\rm if~~}\tilde{\zeta}\leq\frac{1}{2}\\
s_{max}(\zeta,\tilde{\zeta})&,~~{\rm if~~}\tilde{\zeta}>\frac{1}{2}\end{cases}
\]
The quantity \(s_X\) is the entropy of the pure black hole at the intersection; \(s_{max}\) is the larger two-component maximum. Exchanging the electric charges extends the transition to negative \(\tilde\zeta\). Thus sufficiently unequal charges change the phase dominating the predicted index.

title: Phases of Supersymmetric Ground States in AdS₄
text:
Interpretation and limits



Original Figure 15: In the physical wedge \(|\tilde\zeta|\leq\zeta\), the predicted index is dominated by a pure black hole in grey and a two-component configuration in blue. The boundaries lie at \(|\tilde\zeta|=1/2\). Reproduced from the paper.


The distinction between two phase diagrams matters. The ground-state diagram fixes all conserved charges; the index diagram groups states along charge-space lines. A two-component configuration can dominate the latter even though a pure black hole exists elsewhere on the same line. Agreement between a black-hole entropy calculation and an index calculation therefore has a restricted domain, rather than establishing that all typical supersymmetric states are isolated black holes.
The paper also studies complex Euclidean BPS black holes and their chemical potentials. The loss of a convergent statistical interpretation tracks the predicted onset of the two-component index phase. However, the Kontsevich–Segal–Witten criterion for allowable complex metrics remains satisfied in the unstable region. In this example that geometric criterion is too weak to diagnose the relevant transition.
The results retain two important qualifications. First, the detailed existence and supersymmetry of the proposed gas-plus-core configurations require further work, including their backreaction. Second, replacing a rapidly oscillating signed sum by its largest entropy contribution is an assumption, often called the unobstructed saddle conjecture. A direct calculation of the boundary three-dimensional index would test the predicted transition independently. Four unequal electric charges, finite-\(N\) effects, and quantum corrections also lie beyond the analysis here.
